---
title: "Bayesian Computation and Diagnostics"
---

## Introduction {#sec-comp-intro}

The three preceding chapters built the multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) model and showed how
its aggregate-data likelihood is an integral of an individual-level integrand against a covariate
distribution (the aggregation theorem, @thm-aggregation), how that integral is computed by quasi-Monte
Carlo (QMC) on the unit hypercube (@thm-hypercube-integration), and how the resulting model is identified
and estimated (@thm-target-population-integral, @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma). Nothing in that development
told us how to actually *fit* the model, nor how to know whether the fit can be trusted. That is the
business of this chapter.

ML-NMR and its unanchored extension are estimated by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), specifically by
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) and its adaptive form the No-U-Turn Sampler, the engine of the Stan
probabilistic programming language (@carpenter2017stan) on which the reference software is built. We
proved in Chapter 8 that HMC (@def-hmc) leaves the target posterior invariant, by way of the
Metropolis-Hastings detailed-balance argument (@thm-mh-stationarity). Invariance is a statement about the
limiting behavior of an idealized chain. A real analysis runs a finite number of finite chains, and faces
two distinct and additive sources of error that a responsible report must certify are small.

The first is the **Monte Carlo error** of the sampler itself: the chains may not have reached the
stationary distribution (lack of convergence), and even at stationarity their draws are autocorrelated, so
a run of length $N$ carries less information than $N$ independent draws. The hierarchical structure of
ML-NMR makes this acute. Random effects on study baselines and on treatment contrasts (@def-random-effects,
@def-exchangeability) introduce a variance parameter $\tau$ whose joint posterior with the effects it
governs has a pathological "funnel" geometry that defeats a naive sampler. Section @sec-comp-param shows
how to remove the funnel by reparameterization, and proves precisely why it works in terms of the leapfrog
geometry of @def-hmc. Sections @sec-comp-rhat and @sec-comp-ess give the two workhorse convergence
diagnostics, the Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic $\hat R$ and the effective sample size,
and derive both from first principles.

The second source is unique to ML-NMR among the methods in this book: a **numerical-integration error**
nested *inside* the likelihood. Every evaluation of the aggregate likelihood approximates an integral by a
finite QMC sum, so the model the sampler actually targets is a perturbation of the intended one. Section
@sec-comp-integration turns the Koksma-Hlawka bound of Chapter 22 (@thm-koksma-hlawka) into an operational
diagnostic and proves the doubling rule that certifies the integration grid is fine enough.

The chapter closes with model comparison. Sections @sec-comp-ic and @sec-comp-psis develop the deviance
information criterion (DIC), the widely applicable information criterion (WAIC), and leave-one-out
cross-validation (LOO-CV), prove the relationships among them as estimates of the same expected predictive
density, and give the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) algorithm that makes LOO-CV computable
without refitting the model. A fully worked diagnostic example, every number checkable by hand, ties the
pieces together in @sec-comp-example. The chapter corresponds to results I.1 to I.6 of the proof catalogue.

Throughout, $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ denotes the full parameter vector, $\mathbf y$ the observed data,
$\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ the prior, $p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol{\xi})$ the likelihood, and
$\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi}\mid\mathbf y)\propto p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol{\xi})\pi(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ the
posterior, as in [Notation](/notation.qmd) and Chapter 8. We write a generic scalar quantity of interest as
$\theta=h(\boldsymbol{\xi})$, for instance a treatment contrast $d_{ab}$ or a marginal probability
$\theta_{\bullet jk}$.

::: {.remark}
**A note on two effective sample sizes.** The symbol $\mathrm{ESS}$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd) is the
effective sample size of a *weighted* sample, $\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2$, which governed the
variance inflation of MAIC in Chapter 18. The effective sample size of an *autocorrelated MCMC chain*,
developed in @sec-comp-ess, is a different quantity with a different formula, and to keep them apart we
write it $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Both answer the same kind of question, "how many independent draws is this
sample worth," but one loses efficiency to unequal weights and the other to serial correlation.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The sampler in one page: HMC, NUTS, warmup, and divergences {#sec-comp-hmc-primer}

Before the diagnostics, a page on the machine they diagnose, for the reader who has fit a model in Stan
but never looked under the hood. None of this is proved here; it recaps Chapter 8 and fixes the
vocabulary the practical remarks below depend on.

*What a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler does.* We cannot write the posterior
$\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$ down in closed form for an ML-NMR model, but we can draw a long
sequence of parameter vectors $\boldsymbol\xi^{(1)},\boldsymbol\xi^{(2)},\dots$ whose histogram
reproduces it. Each draw is proposed from the current one and then accepted or rejected; the accepted
draws are our sample, and any posterior summary, a mean or a credible interval for the contrast
$d_{AC}$, is just an average over them. That is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).

*Why Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.* A random-walk proposal (as in random-walk Metropolis or Gibbs sampling)
staggers blindly, and in the tens of correlated dimensions of an ML-NMR fit almost every proposed step
is rejected, so the sampler barely moves. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) instead treats the negative log
posterior $U(\boldsymbol\xi)=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$ as a landscape and rolls a
frictionless puck across it, using the gradient $\nabla U$ to steer. A single HMC move can travel a long
way across the posterior while rarely being rejected, which is why HMC, not random-walk Metropolis, is
the sampler that makes ML-NMR feasible: random-walk methods die in high dimensions, and HMC uses
gradient information to take long, directed steps.

*How the puck moves: the leapfrog integrator.* The puck's path obeys Newtonian mechanics, which the
computer solves in small time steps of size $\epsilon$, the *step size*, using the leapfrog integrator
of @def-hmc. Each leapfrog step gives the puck's momentum a half-kick from the gradient, drifts its
position, then completes the kick; we write $r$ for that momentum. The single number $\epsilon$ controls
how large each step is, and getting it wrong is the source of the trouble in @sec-comp-param.

*What the No-U-Turn Sampler adds.* Plain HMC needs the user to choose how many leapfrog steps to take
per move. The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) chooses automatically: it keeps stepping until the trajectory
starts to double back on itself (a "U-turn"), so no trajectory-length tuning is required. NUTS is the
algorithm Stan actually runs.

*Warmup versus sampling.* A run has two phases. During *warmup* the sampler is both moving from its
arbitrary starting point toward the region where the posterior mass actually lives (the *typical set*,
which for a high-dimensional posterior is a thin shell away from the mode, so finding the mode and
sampling the posterior are different tasks) and tuning two knobs: the step size $\epsilon$ and a *mass
matrix*, a linear rescaling of the parameters that makes the landscape rounder. Warmup draws are
tuned-away and discarded; only the *post-warmup* draws, taken with the knobs frozen, are kept.
Everything called "$N$ draws" below means post-warmup draws.

*Divergent transitions.* When the landscape has a region of very sharp curvature, a fixed step size
$\epsilon$ is too coarse to follow it: the leapfrog puck flies off, the simulated energy jumps by more
than a set threshold, and Stan records a *divergent transition*. A divergence is not a rounding
nuisance; it flags a part of the posterior the sampler could not enter, so that region is under-sampled
and any summary that depends on it, often the heterogeneity $\tau$ and the effects tied to it, can be
biased. Even a handful of divergences after warmup must be explained, not ignored. The rest of
@sec-comp-param is, at bottom, the story of where these divergences come from and how a change of
coordinates removes them.

The vocabulary in one place:

| Term | One-line meaning |
|---|---|
| MCMC | draw a dependent sequence whose histogram is the posterior |
| HMC | gradient-guided proposals that move far with few rejections |
| NUTS | HMC that picks its own trajectory length; the Stan default |
| step size $\epsilon$ | how large each leapfrog step is; too large diverges, too small crawls |
| mass matrix | a rescaling of parameters learned in warmup to round out the geometry |
| warmup | the discarded tuning phase; the rest are post-warmup draws |
| typical set | the region carrying the posterior mass, where the sampler should live |
| divergent transition | a step the integrator could not follow; a flag of unexplored geometry |

## A running example: a two-study evidence network {#sec-comp-running}

Every diagnostic below is illustrated on one small network, carried from section to section so that the
abstractions attach to something concrete. It is the smallest network that still has all the features
that make ML-NMR computation delicate.

*The data.* Two randomized trials inform a plaque psoriasis indirect comparison with a binary outcome,
achieving a $75\%$ reduction in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (a "PASI 75 response").

- **Study $AB$** compares treatment $A$ (control) with treatment $B$ and reports **individual patient
  data (IPD)**: for each of its patients we have the treatment arm, the outcome, and two baseline
  covariates, age and disease severity, each centered and scaled.
- **Study $BC$** compares $B$ with $C$ and reports only **aggregate data (AgD)**: per arm, the number of
  responders out of the arm total, plus the arm's mean age and mean severity.

The network is the chain from $A$ to $B$ to $C$: $B$ is the common comparator, so the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast
$d_{AC}$ is estimated only *indirectly*, by combining the within-study contrasts. This is exactly the
ITC problem of Parts III and IV, now fit as one ML-NMR model.

*The model.* On the log-odds (logit) scale the linear predictor for a patient with covariates $\mathbf
x$ on arm $k$ in study $j$ is, as in [Notation](/notation.qmd),
$$
\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x)=\mu_j+\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\mathbf x+\gamma_k+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^\top\mathbf x,
$$
with the convention $\gamma_k=0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0$ on the reference arm, study
baselines $\mu_{AB},\mu_{BC}$, prognostic effects $\boldsymbol\beta_1$, a treatment main effect
$\gamma_k$, and age-and-severity effect modifiers $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$. The study-level relative effects
are given a random-effects distribution with heterogeneity scale $\tau$ (the NMA layer of
@def-random-effects-ma).

*Why this network stresses every diagnostic.* It has exactly **one study per contrast**. That single
fact drives the whole chapter:

- No contrast is replicated, so the likelihood carries essentially no information about $\tau$: its
  posterior is close to its prior and reaches toward $0$, which is the funnel of @sec-comp-param, so the fit
  needs the non-centered parameterization and a carefully justified prior on $\tau$.
- The **aggregate** study $BC$ contributes to the likelihood only through an integral of the
  individual-level response over its covariate distribution, a two-dimensional integral over age and
  severity that must be done by QMC (@sec-comp-integration).
- With so few studies, one of them can dominate: the $\widehat k$ diagnostic of PSIS-LOO
  (@sec-comp-psis) will tell us whether $d_{AC}$ rests on a single study.
- And we will want to compare models, for instance with and without the age effect modifier
  $\boldsymbol\beta_{2}$, which is the job of WAIC and LOO (@sec-comp-ic).

Keep this network in mind: at each transition we return to it and read the diagnostic in its terms.

## Centered and non-centered parameterizations {#sec-comp-param}

The random-effects layer of an ML-NMR model is, at its core, the normal hierarchy of Chapter 8: a vector
of study- or contrast-level effects drawn from a common population distribution whose scale $\tau$ is itself
estimated. We isolate that layer and study how the *algebraic form* in which it is written to the sampler
changes the geometry HMC must traverse, even though it cannot change the posterior distribution. This is
the content of catalogue result I.1.

Here is the problem in one picture, before any algebra. In our running network $\tau$ is the scale of
the random treatment contrast, estimated from a single pair of studies, so the posterior lets $\tau$
wander close to $0$. Plot the draws of a study effect $\theta_j$ against $\log\tau$. The cloud is shaped
like a trumpet bell, or a funnel: wide at the top, where $\tau$ is large and the effects $\theta_j$
range freely, and pinched to a needle at the bottom, where $\tau$ is small and every $\theta_j$ is
forced close to the common mean $\mu$. A sampler exploring this shape must take large steps in the wide
mouth and minute steps in the narrow neck. A single step size cannot do both: tuned for the mouth it
flies out of the neck and diverges; tuned for the neck it crawls hopelessly in the mouth. That mismatch
is the whole pathology, and the fix is to change coordinates so the funnel becomes a cylinder. The two
coordinate systems are the centered and non-centered parameterizations.

::: {#def-centered-noncentered}
## Centered and non-centered parameterization
Consider the normal hierarchy for effects $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J$ with population mean $\mu$ and scale
$\tau>0$,
$$
\theta_j \mid \mu,\tau \sim \mathcal N(\mu,\tau^2), \qquad j=1,\dots,J,
$$ {#eq-comp-hier}
embedded in a model whose remaining likelihood depends on the $\theta_j$ through data terms.

- The **centered parameterization** (CP) takes the unknowns to be $(\mu,\tau,\theta_1,\dots,\theta_J)$
  themselves, so that @eq-comp-hier enters the prior directly.
- The **non-centered parameterization** (NCP) takes the unknowns to be $(\mu,\tau,\tilde\theta_1,\dots,
  \tilde\theta_J)$ with standardized effects
  $$
  \tilde\theta_j \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\ \text{ a priori}, \qquad
  \theta_j := \mu + \tau\,\tilde\theta_j,
  $$ {#eq-comp-ncp}
  and the data terms are written as functions of the deterministic transform $\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j$.
  $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Both parameterizations describe the identical statistical model and give the
identical answer; they differ only in *what the sampler is asked to move around in*. The centered form
(CP) samples the effects $\theta_j$ directly. The non-centered form (NCP) samples standardized shocks
$\tilde\theta_j$ of fixed unit scale and *reconstructs* $\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j$ afterward, so
the width of the effect is carried by $\tau$ rather than baked into the coordinate. The point of the
section is that this cosmetic-looking choice decides whether HMC sees a funnel or a cylinder.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The two are the *same model*: @eq-comp-ncp is an invertible change of variables that carries the standard
normal prior on $\tilde\theta_j$ to the $\mathcal N(\mu,\tau^2)$ prior on $\theta_j$. We record this
precisely, because the equivalence is what licenses choosing between them on purely computational grounds.

::: {#lem-comp-reparam}
## The two parameterizations define one posterior
Fix $(\mu,\tau)$ with $\tau>0$. The map $T_{\mu,\tau}:\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}\mapsto\boldsymbol\theta$
defined by $\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j$ is a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^J$ with constant Jacobian
determinant $\tau^{J}$. The CP joint density in $(\mu,\tau,\boldsymbol\theta)$ and the NCP joint density in
$(\mu,\tau,\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta})$ are related by this change of variables, and the two analyses return
identical posteriors for every quantity $h(\mu,\tau,\boldsymbol\theta)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For fixed $(\mu,\tau)$ the map is affine with linear part $\tau I_J$, hence a bijection of $\mathbb R^J$
with Jacobian matrix $\tau I_J$ and determinant $\tau^J\neq 0$; it is its own smooth inverse
$\tilde\theta_j=(\theta_j-\mu)/\tau$, so it is a diffeomorphism. Writing $\varphi$ for the standard normal
density, the NCP prior on $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$ is $\prod_j\varphi(\tilde\theta_j)$. Pushing it
forward through $T_{\mu,\tau}$ by the change-of-variables formula gives, at $\boldsymbol\theta=
T_{\mu,\tau}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta})$,
$$
\prod_{j}\varphi(\tilde\theta_j)\cdot\left|\det \tfrac{\partial\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}}{\partial
\boldsymbol\theta}\right|
=\prod_{j}\varphi\!\Big(\tfrac{\theta_j-\mu}{\tau}\Big)\cdot\tau^{-J}
=\prod_{j}\mathcal N(\theta_j;\mu,\tau^2),
$$
which is exactly the CP prior. Because the likelihood is written in both as a function of the same
numbers $\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j$, and the priors on $(\mu,\tau)$ are shared, the joint densities
agree under the transform. A diffeomorphic reparameterization leaves all integrals, hence all posterior
expectations and quantiles of any $h$, invariant. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the proof is saying, in words.** A *diffeomorphism* is just a change of variables that is smooth
and smoothly invertible, so no information is lost or created by switching between $\boldsymbol\theta$
and $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. The *change-of-variables formula* is the multivariable version of the
$u$-substitution from calculus: when you rewrite a density in new coordinates you must multiply by the
*Jacobian* factor (here the constant $\tau^{-J}$) to keep total probability equal to one. Because that
bookkeeping is exact, every probability, mean, and credible interval is identical in the two
coordinates. This is the license we need: we may pick the parameterization purely for how well the
sampler moves, with no effect on the reported treatment contrast.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

If the posteriors are identical, why does the choice matter? Because HMC does not sample the posterior
directly; it simulates Hamiltonian trajectories whose stability and step size are dictated by the local
*curvature* of the negative log density, and curvature is not invariant under reparameterization. We make
this quantitative. Recall from @def-hmc that HMC sets $U(\boldsymbol\xi)=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y)$ (the "potential energy") and advances the state by the leapfrog integrator with a single global step
size $\epsilon$. The behavior of the leapfrog integrator on a quadratic potential is the whole story, and
it is governed by one number.

To keep the section self-contained, recall the leapfrog integrator explicitly. It advances a position
$x$ and its momentum $r$ by a step of size $\epsilon$ in three substeps: a half-kick of the momentum by
the gradient, $r^{+}=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}U'(x)$; a full drift of the position, $x'=x+\epsilon r^{+}$;
and a second half-kick, $r'=r^{+}-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}U'(x')$. The momentum $r$ is the auxiliary
"velocity" HMC gives the puck, and $\epsilon$ is the same step size the sampler tunes in warmup. The next
lemma analyzes this map on the simplest possible landscape, a parabola, because near any smooth mode the
landscape *is* a parabola to second order; the one inequality it produces, the largest step the
integrator can survive, is what governs both the funnel pathology and its non-centered cure. That is why
a page on a harmonic oscillator earns its place: it is the single fact the entire section turns on.

::: {#lem-comp-leapfrog-stability}
## Linear stability of the leapfrog integrator
Let $U(x)=\tfrac12\omega^2 x^2$ be a one-dimensional harmonic potential with frequency $\omega>0$ and unit
mass. One leapfrog step of size $\epsilon$ (as in @def-hmc) acts on the state $(x,r)$ as the linear map
$(x',r')^\top=A(x,r)^\top$ with
$$
A=\begin{pmatrix} 1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2 & \epsilon \\[2pt]
-\epsilon\omega^2\big(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2\big) & 1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det A=1 .
$$ {#eq-comp-leapfrog-matrix}
The iterates $A^n$ remain bounded (the integrator is *stable*) if and only if $\epsilon\omega<2$; for
$\epsilon\omega>2$ they grow geometrically, and at $\epsilon\omega=2$ linearly, so the simulated trajectory
diverges.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $U'(x)=\omega^2 x$, the three leapfrog substeps of @def-hmc read
$r^{+}=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x$, then $x'=x+\epsilon r^{+}=(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)x+
\epsilon r$, then $r'=r^{+}-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x'$. Substituting $x'$ into the last line,
$$
r'=r-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2 x-\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\omega^2\big[(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)x+\epsilon
r\big]
=\big(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2\big)r-\epsilon\omega^2\big(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2\big)x,
$$
which is @eq-comp-leapfrog-matrix. Its determinant is
$(1-\tfrac12\epsilon^2\omega^2)^2+\epsilon\cdot\epsilon\omega^2(1-\tfrac14\epsilon^2\omega^2)
=1-\epsilon^2\omega^2+\tfrac14\epsilon^4\omega^4+\epsilon^2\omega^2-\tfrac14\epsilon^4\omega^4=1$,
confirming the volume preservation of @def-hmc. Writing $s=\epsilon\omega$, the trace is $2-s^2$, so the
eigenvalues of $A$ solve $\lambda^2-(2-s^2)\lambda+1=0$ with discriminant $(2-s^2)^2-4=s^2(s^2-4)$. If
$s<2$ the discriminant is negative, the eigenvalues are complex conjugates, and since their product is
$\det A=1$ they have modulus $1$; the powers $A^n$ are then conjugate to a rotation and stay bounded. If
$s>2$ the discriminant is positive, the eigenvalues are real with product $1$, so one exceeds $1$ in
modulus and $A^n$ grows like that eigenvalue to the $n$; the trajectory diverges. At $s=2$ the matrix has a
defective double eigenvalue $-1$ and $\|A^n\|$ grows linearly. Hence stability holds exactly for
$\epsilon\omega<2$. $\square$
:::

The frequency $\omega$ in @lem-comp-leapfrog-stability is $\sqrt{U''(x)}$, the square root of the local
curvature of the potential. The lemma therefore says: the largest usable leapfrog step at a point is
$\epsilon\lesssim 2/\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}$, where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian
$\nabla^2 U$ there. A *single* global $\epsilon$ can be efficient only if this curvature is roughly
constant across the region the chain must visit. The next lemma computes the curvature in the two
parameterizations and exposes the funnel.

::: {#lem-comp-funnel}
## Funnel curvature of the centered hierarchy
Consider @eq-comp-hier with a single weakly-informed effect $\theta_j$ whose data term contributes
curvature $c_j\ge 0$ in $\theta_j$ (so $c_j$ is the negative second derivative of the data log-likelihood
in $\theta_j$, a measure of how firmly the data pin down $\theta_j$; when the data are weakly
informative the likelihood is nearly flat in $\theta_j$, its second derivative is near zero, and
$c_j\to 0$, the prior-dominated limit). Holding $(\mu,\tau)$ fixed:

1. In the centered parameterization the curvature of $U$ in the $\theta_j$ direction is
   $$
   \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial\theta_j^2}=\frac{1}{\tau^2}+c_j .
   $$ {#eq-comp-cp-curv}
2. In the non-centered parameterization the curvature of $U$ in the $\tilde\theta_j$ direction is
   $$
   \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial\tilde\theta_j^2}=1+\tau^2 c_j .
   $$ {#eq-comp-ncp-curv}
:::

::: {.proof}
The potential is $U=-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)=-\log(\text{prior})-\log(\text{likelihood})+
\text{const}$. In CP the prior term involving $\theta_j$ is $-\log\mathcal N(\theta_j;\mu,\tau^2)=
\frac{(\theta_j-\mu)^2}{2\tau^2}+\text{const}$, whose second derivative in $\theta_j$ is $1/\tau^2$; the
data term adds $c_j$ by definition, giving @eq-comp-cp-curv. In NCP the prior term involving
$\tilde\theta_j$ is $-\log\mathcal N(\tilde\theta_j;0,1)=\tfrac12\tilde\theta_j^2+\text{const}$, second
derivative $1$; the data term is the same function of $\theta_j=\mu+\tau\tilde\theta_j$, and by the chain
rule its second derivative in $\tilde\theta_j$ is $(\partial\theta_j/\partial\tilde\theta_j)^2$ times its
second derivative in $\theta_j$, that is $\tau^2 c_j$. Summing gives @eq-comp-ncp-curv. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-comp-param}
## Why the parameterization changes HMC geometry
In the prior-dominated regime $c_j\to 0$ (a study or contrast about which the data are weakly informative):

1. **(Centered funnels.)** The CP curvature @eq-comp-cp-curv is $1/\tau^2$, so by
   @lem-comp-leapfrog-stability the largest stable leapfrog step in the $\theta_j$ direction is
   $\epsilon_{\max}(\tau)=2\tau$, which tends to $0$ as $\tau\to 0$. The posterior of $(\theta_j,\log\tau)$
   is a "funnel," narrowing without bound as $\tau\downarrow 0$; no single global $\epsilon$ is both stable
   in the neck of the funnel and efficient in its mouth.
2. **(Non-centered uniformizes.)** The NCP curvature @eq-comp-ncp-curv is $1$, independent of $\tau$, so the
   largest stable step is $\epsilon_{\max}=2$ for every $\tau$. The funnel is removed and a single step
   size suffices.

In the data-dominated regime $\tau^2 c_j\gg 1$ (many informative studies, well-identified $\tau$) the
roles reverse: NCP couples $\tilde\theta_j$ to $\tau$ through the data term @eq-comp-ncp-curv and can mix
worse than CP, whose curvature @eq-comp-cp-curv is then the well-conditioned $c_j$. The practical rule is
to use NCP when $\tau$ is weakly identified (few studies) and CP when it is strongly identified.
:::

::: {.proof}
Both claims are immediate from substituting the limiting curvatures of @lem-comp-funnel into the stability
threshold $\epsilon_{\max}=2/\omega=2/\sqrt{\text{curvature}}$ of @lem-comp-leapfrog-stability. For (1),
curvature $1/\tau^2$ gives $\omega=1/\tau$ and $\epsilon_{\max}=2\tau\to 0$; because $\tau$ itself ranges
over an interval reaching toward $0$ under the posterior, the step size that is stable at the smallest
visited $\tau$ is far smaller than the step size that is efficient at typical $\tau$, and HMC with one
$\epsilon$ must compromise. The Metropolis correction of @thm-mh-stationarity guards correctness by
rejecting the divergent proposals that an over-large step produces in the neck, but at the cost of a
collapse in acceptance and in distance traveled, which is observed in practice as "divergent transitions."
For (2), curvature $1$ gives $\epsilon_{\max}=2$ for all $\tau$, so stability is uniform over the funnel.
The reversal in the data-dominated regime is the same computation read in the other direction: when
$\tau^2 c_j\gg 1$ the NCP curvature @eq-comp-ncp-curv grows with $\tau$ while the CP curvature
@eq-comp-cp-curv approaches the constant $c_j$, so CP is the better-conditioned coordinate. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and a map of the two regimes.** The theorem is the rigorous version of "change
coordinates so the funnel becomes a cylinder," and it also warns that the cure can become the disease
when the data are strong. The table records both regimes; "curvature" is the second derivative of $U$
that @lem-comp-leapfrog-stability turns into a maximum stable step $\epsilon_{\max}=2/\sqrt{\text{curv}}$.

| Regime | Centered curvature | Non-centered curvature | Better coordinate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weak data ($c_j\to 0$), $\tau$ near $0$ (the neck) | $1/\tau^2$, blows up | $1$, constant | non-centered |
| Weak data, $\tau$ large (the mouth) | $1/\tau^2$, tiny | $1$, constant | either |
| Strong data ($\tau^2 c_j\gg 1$) | $c_j$, well conditioned | $\tau^2 c_j$, grows | centered |

For an indirect comparison this reads directly off the evidence network. Our running network has one
study per contrast, so $\tau$ is weakly identified and its posterior reaches into the neck: it is a
non-centered problem, and fitting it centered would produce divergences clustered at small $\tau$ and an
untrustworthy heterogeneity estimate. A dense network with many studies per contrast identifies $\tau$
strongly and belongs in the bottom row, where the centered form mixes better.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The funnel in ML-NMR.** In ML-NMR the effects $\theta_j$ are the random treatment contrasts
$\delta_{j,1k}$ (the random-effects NMA layer, @def-random-effects-ma), and the study baselines $\mu_j$ when
they too are given a random-effects distribution (by default they are fixed effects). Networks with
few studies per contrast, the norm in health-technology-assessment submissions, sit squarely in the
prior-dominated regime, where @thm-comp-param prescribes the non-centered form. The reference software
implements the non-centered parameterization by default for exactly this reason; the diagnostic signature
of a residual funnel is a cluster of divergent transitions concentrated at small $\tau$, visible in a
scatter plot of any $\theta_j$ against $\log\tau$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.1 in the proof catalogue.

## The Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction statistic {#sec-comp-rhat}

Reparameterization makes the chains mix; diagnostics tell us whether they have. The first question is
convergence: have the chains forgotten their starting points and settled to a common stationary
distribution? The standard answer compares the spread of several independently started chains to the
spread within each. If the chains agree, the between-chain spread is no larger than the within; if they
have not converged, the between-chain spread is inflated. The Gelman-Rubin statistic makes this a number.
This is catalogue result I.2, which we derive in full.

**The bottom line first.** The statistic is $\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}$, the ratio of a pooled,
all-chains-together estimate of the posterior spread $\widehat V$ to the average within-chain spread $W$.
Read it as a single question: *are the separate chains telling the same posterior story?* If they are,
the two spreads agree and $\widehat R$ sits at $1$; if the chains have settled in different places or are
still drifting, the pooled spread is inflated and $\widehat R$ rises above $1$. The working rule is to
require $\widehat R\le 1.01$ for every reported quantity. In the running example that means checking it
not only on the headline contrast $d_{AC}$ but on $\tau$, the study baselines $\mu_{AB},\mu_{BC}$, the
effect modifier $\boldsymbol\beta_2$, and the transformed marginal probabilities you report; the
heterogeneity $\tau$ is usually the last to converge and the one to watch. The rest of this section
proves why this ratio has exactly that behavior; a reader who trusts the rule can skim to @sec-comp-ess
on a first pass.

Throughout this section we have $M\ge 2$ chains, each of post-warmup length $N$, with draws
$\theta^{(m,t)}$ for chain $m=1,\dots,M$ and iteration $t=1,\dots,N$, of a scalar quantity
$\theta=h(\boldsymbol\xi)$.

::: {#def-comp-rhat-pieces}
## Within-chain, between-chain, and pooled variance estimators
With chain means $\bar\theta^{(m)}=\frac1N\sum_t\theta^{(m,t)}$ and grand mean
$\bar{\bar\theta}=\frac1M\sum_m\bar\theta^{(m)}$, define
$$
W=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^{M}s_m^2,\quad s_m^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\big(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)}
\big)^2;\qquad
B=\frac{N}{M-1}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\big(\bar\theta^{(m)}-\bar{\bar\theta}\big)^2 ;
$$ {#eq-comp-wb}
the **within-chain variance** $W$ (the average of the per-chain sample variances) and the **between-chain
variance** $B$ (the sample variance of the chain means, scaled by $N$). The **pooled marginal-variance
estimator** is
$$
\widehat V=\Big(1-\tfrac1N\Big)W+\tfrac1N B .
$$ {#eq-comp-vhat}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** $W$ asks how much a *single* chain wiggles around its own average; $B$ asks how
far the *chain averages* sit from one another. If the chains have converged to the same distribution
these measure the same spread, so their combination $\widehat V$ neither over- nor under-states the
posterior variance. If the chains disagree, $B$ is inflated by the disagreement while $W$ is not, and the
ratio $\widehat V/W$ climbs above $1$. The scaling by $N$ in $B$ is what puts the between-chain and
within-chain pieces on the same footing.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The rationale for these particular combinations is not obvious from the formulas. We supply it with two
exact expectation identities, valid under an explicit idealization of what "converged" means, and then
read off the behavior of the statistic.

::: {#lem-comp-within}
## Expectation of the within-chain variance
Suppose each chain is *second-order stationary*, meaning its mean is constant along the chain and the
covariance between two draws depends only on how many iterations separate them, not on where in the
chain they sit, with marginal variance $\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(\theta)$, and
let $v_N=\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta^{(m)})$ be the variance of a single chain mean. Then $\mathbb E[s_m^2]=
\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)$, and hence
$$
\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big).
$$ {#eq-comp-ew}
:::

::: {.proof}
Let $m_0=\mathbb E[\theta^{(m,t)}]$, constant in $t$ by stationarity. Using
$\sum_t(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)})^2=\sum_t\theta^{(m,t)2}-N\bar\theta^{(m)2}$ and taking
expectations,
$$
\mathbb E\!\Big[\textstyle\sum_t(\theta^{(m,t)}-\bar\theta^{(m)})^2\Big]
=\sum_t\big(\sigma^2+m_0^2\big)-N\big(v_N+m_0^2\big)
=N\sigma^2-Nv_N ,
$$
because $\mathbb E[\theta^{(m,t)2}]=\mathrm{Var}(\theta^{(m,t)})+m_0^2=\sigma^2+m_0^2$ and
$\mathbb E[\bar\theta^{(m)2}]=v_N+m_0^2$. Dividing by $N-1$ gives $\mathbb E[s_m^2]=\frac{N}{N-1}
(\sigma^2-v_N)$, and averaging over the $M$ chains gives @eq-comp-ew. $\square$
:::

::: {#lem-comp-between}
## Expectation of the between-chain variance
Suppose in addition that the $M$ chains are mutually independent and share the common stationary
distribution (in particular a common mean). Then
$$
\mathbb E[B]=N v_N .
$$ {#eq-comp-eb}
:::

::: {.proof}
Under the stated assumptions the chain means $\bar\theta^{(1)},\dots,\bar\theta^{(M)}$ are independent and
identically distributed with common variance $v_N$. The quantity $\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m(\bar\theta^{(m)}-
\bar{\bar\theta})^2$ is the ordinary sample variance of these $M$ numbers, which is an unbiased estimator
of their common variance $v_N$. Multiplying by $N$, as in the definition @eq-comp-wb of $B$, gives
$\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-gelman-rubin}
## Gelman-Rubin potential scale reduction
Define the **potential scale reduction factor**
$$
\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}.
$$ {#eq-comp-rhat}

1. **(Unbiasedness of $\widehat V$ at stationarity.)** Under the idealization of @lem-comp-within and
   @lem-comp-between (independent chains sharing one stationary law of finite variance $\sigma^2$), the
   pooled estimator is exactly unbiased for the marginal posterior variance,
   $$
   \mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2 ,
   $$
   for every $N$ and every within-chain autocorrelation structure.

2. **(One-sided bias and the limit.)** For chains with non-negative autocorrelations,
   $\mathbb E[\widehat V]\ge\mathbb E[W]$, with
   $$
   \mathbb E[\widehat V]-\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N v_N-\sigma^2}{N-1}\ge 0 ,
   $$ {#eq-comp-gap}
   so $\widehat R$ is centered at or above $1$; and if the chains are ergodic, so that $v_N\to 0$ and
   $Nv_N\to\sigma^2\big(1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k\big)$ as $N\to\infty$, then $\mathbb E[W]\to\sigma^2$ and
   $\widehat R\xrightarrow{p}1$.

3. **(Detection of non-convergence.)** If the chains are stationary but with *different* means
   $m_1,\dots,m_M$ (over-dispersed starting points not yet forgotten, or distinct posterior modes), then
   $$
   \mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{m}\big(m_m-\bar m\big)^2,
   \qquad \bar m=\tfrac1M\textstyle\sum_m m_m ,
   $$
   while $\mathbb E[W]$ is unchanged at $\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)$; the extra between-mean dispersion
   inflates $\widehat V/W$ above $1$ and does not vanish as $N\to\infty$ unless the means coincide.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* By @eq-comp-vhat and linearity of expectation,
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\Big(1-\tfrac1N\Big)\mathbb E[W]+\tfrac1N\mathbb E[B]
=\frac{N-1}{N}\cdot\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)+\frac1N\cdot N v_N
=\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)+v_N=\sigma^2,
$$
using @eq-comp-ew and @eq-comp-eb. The cancellation is exact and uses no assumption on the
autocorrelations beyond second-order stationarity.

*Part 2.* Subtracting @eq-comp-ew from $\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2$,
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat V]-\mathbb E[W]=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{N-1}\big(\sigma^2-v_N\big)
=\frac{(N-1)\sigma^2-N\sigma^2+Nv_N}{N-1}=\frac{Nv_N-\sigma^2}{N-1}.
$$
Now $v_N=\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta^{(m)})=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\big)$
by the variance-of-the-mean identity @prp-comp-acf-variance (proved independently in @sec-comp-ess,
using nothing from this section, so there is no circular dependence), so
$Nv_N=\sigma^2\big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\big)\ge
\sigma^2$ whenever every $\rho_k\ge 0$; the gap @eq-comp-gap is therefore non-negative, which gives
$\mathbb E[\widehat V]\ge\mathbb E[W]$, so $\widehat R$ is centered at or above $1$. For the limit,
ergodicity makes $v_N\to 0$, so $\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)\to\sigma^2$ as well (equivalently, the gap
@eq-comp-gap is $\frac{\sigma^2\cdot 2\sum_k(1-k/N)\rho_k}{N-1}\to 0$ because the bracket converges to the
finite constant $\sum_k\rho_k$); both $\widehat V$ and $W$ converge to $\sigma^2$ and their ratio to $1$.

*Part 3.* When the chains have different means, the chain means $\bar\theta^{(m)}$ are independent with
$\mathbb E[\bar\theta^{(m)}]=m_m$ and variance $v_N$. The sample variance of independent variables with
unequal means decomposes into the average variance plus the sample variance of the means: taking
expectations in $\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m(\bar\theta^{(m)}-\bar{\bar\theta})^2$ gives $v_N+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m
(m_m-\bar m)^2$. Hence $\mathbb E[B]=Nv_N+\frac{N}{M-1}\sum_m(m_m-\bar m)^2$, and
$$
\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\frac{N-1}{N}\mathbb E[W]+\frac1N\mathbb E[B]
=\sigma^2+\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_m\big(m_m-\bar m\big)^2 .
$$
The within-chain expectation @eq-comp-ew is untouched because it never references the cross-chain means.
The extra term is a fixed positive constant independent of $N$, so $\widehat V/W$ stays bounded away from
$1$ as $N$ grows, which is the diagnostic firing. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and the three ways $\widehat R$ fails.** For an indirect comparison, a large
$\widehat R$ on the contrast $d_{AC}$ means the estimate is not yet stable: rerun the analysis with a
different seed and you could get a materially different number, which is indefensible in a reimbursement
submission. Part 3 of the theorem is the precise reason, and it fires in three recognizable patterns.
(i) *Different modes*: the chains settle in genuinely different places, for example a bimodal posterior
for an effect modifier, so the chain means $m_m$ differ and the extra term in Part 3 never vanishes.
(ii) *Slow drift*: a chain has not reached the typical set and is still trending, which split-$\widehat
R$ (below) is designed to catch by comparing each chain's two halves. (iii) *One rogue chain*: a single
chain stuck in the funnel neck while the others mix, dragging one $m_m$ away from the rest. In all three
the action is the same: do not read the posterior yet. Diagnose which parameter is bad and treat the
cause, usually more warmup, the non-centered parameterization of @sec-comp-param, or a tighter prior on
$\tau$, rather than simply running longer.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading $\widehat R$, and modern refinements.** Part 1 is the classical fact that $\widehat V$
*overestimates* the posterior variance when the chains start over-dispersed (Part 3) and is unbiased once
they have mixed (Part 1), while $W$ *underestimates* it until each chain has explored the whole support
(Part 2); $\widehat R$ compresses both failures into a single number that descends to $1$. The widely used
threshold is $\widehat R\le 1.01$ for every reported quantity. Two refinements are now standard: *split-
$\widehat R$* divides each chain into two halves and treats them as separate chains, so that within-chain
non-stationarity (a slow trend) inflates the between-chain term and is detected; and *rank-normalized*
$\widehat R$ applies the statistic to the normal scores of the pooled ranks, which makes it well defined
for heavy-tailed or infinite-variance targets where $\sigma^2$ in @thm-gelman-rubin would not exist. The
rank-normalized version and the $1.01$ threshold are due to @vehtari2021rhat, and both refinements are the
defaults in current software.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.2 in the proof catalogue.

## Effective sample size for autocorrelated chains {#sec-comp-ess}

A chain can be perfectly converged ($\widehat R=1$) and still nearly useless if its draws are highly
correlated, because correlated draws carry redundant information. The effective sample size quantifies
exactly how many independent draws the chain is worth for estimating a posterior expectation. This is
catalogue result I.3. The development rests on one exact variance identity for the mean of a stationary
sequence, which we also used in @thm-gelman-rubin.

::: {#prp-comp-acf-variance}
## Variance of the mean of a stationary chain
Let $\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(N)}$ be second-order stationary with variance $\sigma^2$ and lag-$k$
autocorrelation $\rho_k=\mathrm{Corr}(\theta^{(t)},\theta^{(t+k)})$. Then
$$
\mathrm{Var}\big(\bar\theta_N\big)=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}\Big(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\Big(1-\frac kN\Big)\rho_k
\Big),\qquad \bar\theta_N=\frac1N\sum_{t=1}^N\theta^{(t)} .
$$ {#eq-comp-var-mean}
If moreover $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\rho_k|<\infty$, then $N\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\to\sigma^2\,
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ as $N\to\infty$, where $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_k$ is the
**integrated autocorrelation time**.
:::

::: {.proof}
Expanding the variance of the sum and using stationarity, $\mathrm{Cov}(\theta^{(s)},\theta^{(t)})=
\sigma^2\rho_{|s-t|}$, so
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{s=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^N\sigma^2\rho_{|s-t|}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{N^2}\Big(N+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\rho_k\Big),
$$
because the lag $|s-t|=0$ occurs for the $N$ diagonal pairs and each lag $k\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$ occurs for
$2(N-k)$ ordered pairs. Factoring $N$ out of the bracket gives @eq-comp-var-mean. For the limit, each
summand $(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\to\rho_k$ pointwise as $N\to\infty$ and is dominated by $|\rho_k|$, which is
summable by hypothesis; dominated convergence gives $\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k\to\sum_{k\ge1}
\rho_k$, hence $N\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)=\sigma^2(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(1-\tfrac kN)\rho_k)\to\sigma^2
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$. $\square$
:::

::: {#def-mcmc-ess}
## Effective sample size of an MCMC chain
For a second-order stationary chain with integrated autocorrelation time $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k
\ge1}\rho_k$, the **effective sample size** for the posterior mean is
$$
N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{N}{\tau_{\mathrm{int}}}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\rho_k}.
$$ {#eq-comp-ess}
With $M$ chains of length $N$ the total is $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=MN/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$. The ratio
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}/N\in(0,1]$ is the chain's **efficiency**. In practice the infinite sum is truncated at
the first lag where the estimated autocorrelations cease to be reliably positive (for example by Geyer's
initial-monotone-sequence rule), because sample autocorrelations at large lags are dominated by noise.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ answers "how many truly independent draws is this correlated
chain worth?" A run of $4000$ draws with $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=4000$ is as good as $4000$ coin flips; one
with $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=200$ carries the information of only $200$. The integrated autocorrelation time
$\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ is the exchange rate: each draw is worth $1/\tau_{\mathrm{int}}$ of an independent
draw. A low $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ does not bias the estimate; it makes it *noisy*, which for an ITC shows up
as jittery credible-interval endpoints on the contrast.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The definition is justified by the property that gives it its name: $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the number of
independent draws that would estimate the posterior mean with the same Monte Carlo variance.

::: {#cor-comp-ess-variance}
## $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ equalizes Monte Carlo variance
Under the summability hypothesis of @prp-comp-acf-variance, the asymptotic Monte Carlo variance of the
chain mean is
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\sim\frac{\sigma^2}{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\qquad(N\to\infty),
$$
the same as the variance $\sigma^2/n$ of a mean of $n=N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ independent draws. The Monte Carlo
standard error of $\bar\theta_N$ is therefore $\sigma/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @prp-comp-acf-variance, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar\theta_N)\sim\sigma^2\tau_{\mathrm{int}}/N=\sigma^2/(N/
\tau_{\mathrm{int}})=\sigma^2/N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from the definition @eq-comp-ess. Equating to the iid
variance $\sigma^2/n$ gives $n=N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and the standard error is the square root. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-comp-ar1}
## Effective sample size of an AR(1) chain
The first-order autoregressive process $\theta^{(t)}=\phi\,\theta^{(t-1)}+\varepsilon_t$ with $|\phi|<1$
and white-noise $\varepsilon_t$ is the canonical model for a sticky MCMC chain; its lag-$k$
autocorrelation is $\rho_k=\phi^{k}$. Summing the geometric series,
$$
\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\phi^k=1+\frac{2\phi}{1-\phi}=\frac{1+\phi}{1-\phi},
\qquad N_{\mathrm{eff}}=N\,\frac{1-\phi}{1+\phi}.
$$
A mildly autocorrelated chain with $\phi=\tfrac13$ has $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=2$ and efficiency $\tfrac12$:
$N=4000$ draws are worth $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2000$. A sticky chain with $\phi=0.9$ has
$\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=19$ and efficiency $1/19$: the same $4000$ draws are worth only $N_{\mathrm{eff}}
\approx 210$, a twentyfold loss. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The same formula, tabulated across stickiness, shows how fast efficiency collapses:

| lag-1 correlation $\phi$ | $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=\tfrac{1+\phi}{1-\phi}$ | efficiency $N_{\mathrm{eff}}/N$ | $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from $N=4000$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ (independent) | $1$ | $1$ | $4000$ |
| $1/3$ | $2$ | $0.50$ | $2000$ |
| $0.6$ | $4$ | $0.25$ | $1000$ |
| $0.9$ | $19$ | $0.053$ | $210$ |
| $0.95$ | $39$ | $0.026$ | $103$ |

The message for an indirect comparison: a chain can pass $\widehat R\le 1.01$ and still be nearly useless
if it is sticky, so $\widehat R$ and $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ must be read together. In the running example a
small $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ on $d_{AC}$ warns that its posterior mean is imprecisely pinned down by Monte
Carlo, and a small *tail* $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (defined next) warns specifically that the $95\%$
credible-interval endpoints reported to the payer are noisy.

::: {.remark}
**Bulk and tail effective sample size.** The estimate @eq-comp-ess targets the posterior *mean*. Posterior
*quantiles*, which determine credible intervals, are governed by the autocorrelation of indicator
functions $\mathbf 1\{\theta^{(t)}\le q\}$ rather than of $\theta^{(t)}$ itself, and can mix far worse,
especially deep in the tails. Current software therefore reports a *bulk* $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (from the
rank-normalized draws, for the center of the distribution) and a *tail* $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ (the minimum of
the effective sizes for the $5\%$ and $95\%$ quantile indicators). A common standard is bulk and tail
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}\ge 400$ across chains for inference, with larger tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ demanded when
extreme quantiles are reported. A small tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ beside a healthy bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is
the signature of a chain that estimates the posterior mean well but its interval endpoints poorly.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.3 in the proof catalogue.

## Monitoring the numerical-integration error {#sec-comp-integration}

We turn to the error peculiar to ML-NMR. Each aggregate-data study contributes to the likelihood through
an integral of the individual-level integrand $g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(\mathbf x))$ over the study's covariate
distribution (the aggregation theorem, @thm-aggregation), and that integral is replaced in computation by
a QMC average over $N$ points on the unit hypercube (@thm-hypercube-integration). The sampler therefore
targets not the exact posterior but its QMC approximation, and we must certify that the substitution is
harmless. This is catalogue result I.4.

Write the exact aggregate-cell quantity as $\theta=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u$, where the
integrand $f=g^{-1}\!\circ\eta_{jk}\circ\Psi$ folds the inverse link, the linear predictor, and the
copula-plus-inverse-CDF transform $\Psi$ of Chapter 22 (@thm-inverse-cdf, @def-gaussian-copula) into a
function on the cube; write $\widehat\theta^{(N)}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(\mathbf u_i)$ for its QMC estimate
on the first $N$ points of a Sobol' sequence (@def-sobol-net). The error is *deterministic* given the
point set, and is controlled by the Koksma-Hlawka inequality of Chapter 22.

In words, and tied to the running network: the aggregate study $BC$ never shows us its patients, only
arm summaries, so to evaluate its likelihood we must average the individual response over the covariate
mix in that arm. The transform $\Psi$ is the recipe that turns a uniform grid point $\mathbf
u\in[0,1]^d$ into a plausible patient's covariate vector (age, severity) drawn from the arm's fitted
distribution; $\eta_{jk}$ then gives that synthetic patient's linear predictor, $g^{-1}$ converts it to
an event probability, and the QMC sum averages over a grid of such patients. So $\theta$ is the arm's
expected event probability and $\widehat\theta^{(N)}$ is our $N$-patient numerical approximation to it.
Two glosses for the symbols carried over from Chapter 22: the *Hardy-Krause variation* $V_{\mathrm{HK}}
(f)$ is a multivariable generalization of total variation, a measure of how much the integrand wiggles
(its room to be mis-sampled by a finite grid), and the *star discrepancy* $D_N^{*}$ measures how
unevenly the $N$ points fill the cube (small discrepancy means they cover it evenly). The Koksma-Hlawka
bound below simply multiplies the two.

::: {.remark}
**The error is bounded, not random.** By @thm-koksma-hlawka, for $f$ of finite Hardy-Krause variation,
$$
\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta\big|\le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)\,D_N^{*}(P_N),
$$ {#eq-comp-kh}
the product of the integrand's variation and the star discrepancy $D_N^{*}$ of the point set $P_N$, which
for a Sobol' net is $O\big((\log N)^d/N\big)$. Unlike the $O(N^{-1/2})$ root-mean-square error of plain
Monte Carlo (@thm-mc-rmse), @eq-comp-kh is a worst-case bound with no probability attached. The
difficulty is that $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(f)$ is unknown and usually uncomputable, so @eq-comp-kh certifies a
rate but not a usable constant. The operational diagnostic below sidesteps it by measuring convergence
empirically. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-integration-error-monitoring}
## Doubling diagnostic for integration error
Let $\widehat\theta^{(N)}$ and $\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}$ be the QMC estimates of an aggregate-cell
quantity using the first $N$ and the first $N/2$ points of the same Sobol' sequence. The estimate is
declared **converged at tolerance $\epsilon$** when the relative doubling increment satisfies
$$
\frac{\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}\big|}{\big|\widehat\theta^{(N)}\big|}<\epsilon
$$ {#eq-comp-doubling}
for every aggregate cell, for a small tolerance such as $\epsilon=0.005$. If the criterion fails for any
cell, $N$ is doubled and the test repeated. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation, and a caution on the denominator.** The rule is the numerical analyst's oldest
trick: if halving the grid barely changes the answer, the answer has stopped moving, so you can stop
refining. The relative form divides by $|\widehat\theta^{(N)}|$ so that "small" means small *compared to
the quantity itself*. That is exactly wrong when the quantity is near zero (a rare-event probability) or
naturally lives on a transformed scale that passes through zero (a log-odds or log-hazard): there the
relative increment blows up for no real reason, and one should switch to an absolute tolerance on the
quantity, or run the test on the probability scale where the target is bounded in $[0,1]$. In the
running example the $BC$ arm's event probability sits comfortably away from $0$ and $1$, so the relative
test is safe; a sparse-outcome cell would call for the absolute version.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The diagnostic measures the *observable* increment $\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}$, whereas
what we care about is the *unobservable* error $\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta$. The following proposition
shows that, whenever the error decays at a definite rate, the observable increment controls the
unobservable error up to a known constant, which is what makes @eq-comp-doubling a valid stopping rule.

::: {#prp-comp-doubling}
## The increment bounds the error under geometric decay
Write $e_N=\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\theta$ for the error and $\Delta_N=\widehat\theta^{(N)}-
\widehat\theta^{(N/2)}=e_N-e_{N/2}$ for the observable increment. Suppose there is a contraction factor
$\rho\in[0,1)$ with $|e_N|\le\rho\,|e_{N/2}|$ along the doubling sequence (a definite convergence rate).
Then
$$
|e_{N/2}|\le\frac{|\Delta_N|}{1-\rho}\qquad\text{and}\qquad |e_N|\le\frac{\rho\,|\Delta_N|}{1-\rho}.
$$ {#eq-comp-error-bound}
Consequently, passing the relative test @eq-comp-doubling certifies a relative integration error of at
most $\tfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\epsilon$ in $\widehat\theta^{(N)}$, to leading order.
:::

::: {.proof}
From $\Delta_N=e_N-e_{N/2}$ and the triangle inequality, $|e_{N/2}|=|e_N-\Delta_N|\le|e_N|+|\Delta_N|\le
\rho|e_{N/2}|+|\Delta_N|$. Rearranging, $(1-\rho)|e_{N/2}|\le|\Delta_N|$, which is the first bound in
@eq-comp-error-bound since $\rho<1$; the second follows from $|e_N|\le\rho|e_{N/2}|$. Dividing by
$|\theta|\approx|\widehat\theta^{(N)}|$ and using @eq-comp-doubling, the relative error is at most
$\tfrac{\rho}{1-\rho}\,\epsilon$ to leading order in the small quantities. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What $\rho$ is for QMC and for Monte Carlo.** For a QMC rule with error envelope $a_N=(\log N)^d/N$, the
ratio of successive errors is $a_N/a_{N/2}=\tfrac12\cdot\big(\tfrac{\log N}{\log N-\log 2}\big)^{d}\to
\tfrac12$ as $N\to\infty$, so $\rho\approx\tfrac12$ in the regime where the logarithmic factor is slowly
varying, and @eq-comp-error-bound gives $|e_N|\lesssim|\Delta_N|$: the increment is itself a good error
estimate. For plain Monte Carlo, $a_N=N^{-1/2}$ gives $a_N/a_{N/2}=1/\sqrt2\approx0.707$, so $\rho\approx
0.707$ and the true error can be roughly $2.4$ times the observed increment, a reminder that the doubling
rule is sharper for QMC than for Monte Carlo. The logarithmic factor means $\rho$ is only asymptotically
$\tfrac12$; in the pre-asymptotic regime one should keep $\epsilon$ conservative, which is why the
recommended tolerances are small. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Practical grid sizes and the combined budget.** Empirically, $N\in\{64,128,256\}$ Sobol' points suffice
for ML-NMR with two to four covariates, and the reference software defaults to $N=64$; high-dimensional
covariate sets ($d>6$) call for $N=256$ or for an Owen-scrambled Sobol' rule, a randomized QMC variant
whose error has better behavior on non-smooth integrands. The total error in a posterior summary is the
sum of the two contributions of this chapter,
$$
\text{total error}\ \approx\ \underbrace{O\big(1/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{eff}}}\big)}_{\text{MCMC error}}
\ +\ \underbrace{O\big((\log N)^d/N\big)}_{\text{QMC error}},
$$
and a credible analysis drives both below the precision required of the reported contrast. The two are
controlled by different levers: longer or better-mixed chains for the first, more integration points for
the second. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why not just use a huge grid?** Because the QMC sum sits *inside* the likelihood. Every one of the
millions of likelihood evaluations that HMC performs, at every leapfrog step of every draw, re-runs the
$N$-point sum for every aggregate cell, so the wall-clock cost of the entire fit scales linearly in $N$:
doubling the grid doubles the run time. The doubling diagnostic exists precisely to find the *smallest*
$N$ that is accurate enough, rather than paying for a large grid everywhere out of caution. For the
running network, with $d=2$ covariates in the $BC$ arm, $N=64$ Sobol' points typically pass the test at
$\epsilon=0.005$; a submission with six or more effect modifiers is where one must check the doubling
rule seriously and may need $N=256$ or an Owen-scrambled rule.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.4 in the proof catalogue.

## Information criteria: DIC, WAIC, and leave-one-out cross-validation {#sec-comp-ic}

We now turn from certifying a single fit to comparing fits. The right currency for Bayesian model
comparison is *out-of-sample predictive accuracy*: how well would the fitted model predict a fresh
observation? All three criteria of this section estimate the same target, the expected log pointwise
predictive density, and the point of the section is to derive how they are related, why two of them
(WAIC and LOO-CV) are nearly identical, and where the third (DIC) sits. This is catalogue result I.5.

Fix the data $\mathbf y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)$ with a likelihood that factors across observations,
$p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$.

::: {.remark}
**What is an observation in ML-NMR?** The index $i$ ranges over whatever units the likelihood factorizes
into, and in a mixed IPD-plus-AgD model these are of two kinds. For the IPD study $AB$ each *individual
patient* is one factor, with $p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ a Bernoulli response probability. For the
aggregate study $BC$ the factor is one *arm's summary*, with $p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ the binomial
probability of that arm's responder count given its integrated (QMC-averaged) event probability. So $n$
counts individual patients from $AB$ plus arm-cells from $BC$, not studies and not contrasts. This choice
of unit is not cosmetic: WAIC's penalty, LOO's held-out density, PSIS's $\widehat k$, and the standard
error of a model-comparison difference are all computed *per factor*, so leaving out unit $i$ means
leaving out one patient (fine-grained, low influence) or one whole aggregate arm (coarse, high
influence). When you read a large $\widehat k$ in this model, first ask whether the flagged unit is a
single patient or an entire aggregate arm.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Write the per-observation log
likelihood as $\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\log p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ and its posterior mean and variance
as
$$
m_i=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)],
\qquad
v_i=\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)].
$$
The posterior predictive density of a held-out replicate is $p(\,\cdot\mid\mathbf y)=\mathbb
E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[p(\,\cdot\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]$ (the posterior predictive distribution of
Chapter 8). The **expected log pointwise predictive density** (elpd) is the target,
$$
\mathrm{elpd}=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_{\tilde y_i}\big[\log p(\tilde y_i\mid\mathbf y)\big],
$$
where $\tilde y_i$ is a new observation from the true data-generating process at the $i$-th design point;
larger elpd means better prediction. Its naive in-sample estimate, evaluating the predictive density at the
observed data, is the **log pointwise predictive density**
$$
\mathrm{lppd}=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\big].
$$ {#eq-comp-lppd}
The lppd is optimistic, because each $y_i$ was used both to form the posterior and to test it. The criteria
differ in how they correct that optimism.

The engine of the section is one exact identity that re-expresses the leave-one-out predictive density as a
posterior expectation under the *full* posterior, so that it can be computed from a single fit.

::: {#lem-comp-loo-identity}
## Leave-one-out importance-sampling identity
Let $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})$ denote the posterior with the $i$-th observation removed. Then
the leave-one-out predictive density is the posterior harmonic mean of the $i$-th likelihood,
$$
p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[\,1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)
\,\big]},
$$ {#eq-comp-loo-identity}
and more generally, for any integrable $\psi$,
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)]
=\frac{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\,r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\big]}
{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\big]},
\qquad r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\frac{1}{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)} .
$$ {#eq-comp-is}
:::

::: {.proof}
*Strategy.* We relate the leave-one-out posterior to the full posterior by a single importance ratio,
then read off the harmonic-mean form by choosing the test function $\psi$ cleverly. Every step is one
line of Bayes' theorem; there is no hidden machinery.

Because the likelihood factors, removing $y_i$ divides the full likelihood by the $i$-th factor, so
$$
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})
=\frac{p(\mathbf y_{-i}\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}
=\frac{p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)}{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,p(\mathbf y_{-i})}
=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\cdot\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)}{p(y_i\mid
\boldsymbol\xi)},
$$
using Bayes' theorem (@thm-conjugate-normal is the conjugate special case; here we use only the
proportionality $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\propto p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\pi(\boldsymbol
\xi)$). Thus the importance ratio of the leave-one-out posterior to the full posterior is
$\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})/\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf
y_{-i})}\,r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)$, proportional to $r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$. For any
$\psi$,
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[\psi]
=\int\psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\,\frac{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})}{\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)}\,
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\,d\boldsymbol\xi
=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\,\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\psi\,r_i] .
$$
Taking $\psi\equiv 1$ gives $1=\frac{p(\mathbf y)}{p(\mathbf y_{-i})}\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y}[r_i]$, which both pins the unknown constant and, on dividing, yields the self-normalized form
@eq-comp-is (self-normalized because the denominator is estimated from the same draws, so the unknown
constant $p(\mathbf y)/p(\mathbf y_{-i})$ cancels and never has to be computed). Finally take
$\psi=p(y_i\mid\cdot)$: the numerator is $\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)\,r_i]=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1]=1$, so
$$
p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i}}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]
=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[r_i]}
=\frac{1}{\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]},
$$
which is @eq-comp-loo-identity. $\square$
:::

With the identity in hand we define the three criteria and prove how they relate. All are written so that
*lower is better*, on the deviance scale (a factor of $-2$ times a log predictive density), to match
historical convention.

::: {#def-comp-criteria}
## DIC, WAIC, and LOO-CV
With $D(\boldsymbol\xi)=-2\log p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ the deviance and $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}=
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\boldsymbol\xi]$ the posterior mean:

- the **deviance information criterion** is $\mathrm{DIC}=D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+2p_{D}$ with effective
  parameter count $p_{D}=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[D(\boldsymbol\xi)]-D(\bar{\boldsymbol
  \xi})$;
- the **widely applicable information criterion** is $\mathrm{WAIC}=-2\big(\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm
  {WAIC}}\big)$ with $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Var}_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid
  \mathbf y}[\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)]$;
- **leave-one-out cross-validation** is $\mathrm{LOO}=-2\,\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}$ with
  $\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\sum_{i=1}^n\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** All three are "fit minus a complexity penalty," on the deviance scale where
lower is better. The first term rewards fitting the data you have; the penalty ($2p_D$, $2p_{\mathrm
{WAIC}}$, or the built-in leave-one-out of LOO) docks you for the optimism of having used each
observation both to fit and to score the model. They differ only in how honestly they estimate that
optimism, which the next theorem quantifies.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-dic-waic-loo}
## Relationships among the predictive criteria
Assume the posterior concentrates as $n\to\infty$ in the standard regular way, so that for each $i$ the
posterior fluctuation of $\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)$ has variance $v_i=O(1/n)$ and third cumulant
$\kappa_{3,i}=o(v_i)$. Then:

1. **(WAIC equals LOO to second order.)** For each observation,
   $$
   \log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\mathrm{lppd}_i-v_i+o(v_i),
   $$ {#eq-comp-waic-loo-pointwise}
   where $\mathrm{lppd}_i=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]$.
   Summing, $\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}+o(1)$, so
   $\mathrm{WAIC}=\mathrm{LOO}+o(1)$.

2. **(DIC's effective parameters.)** For an approximately quadratic log likelihood with observed
   information $\mathcal J=-\nabla^2\log p(\mathbf y\mid\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$ (the curvature of the log
   likelihood at the posterior mean, the sample analogue of the Fisher information of Chapter 5),
   $$
   p_{D}=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1),
   $$ {#eq-comp-pd}
   which under a flat prior, where the Bernstein-von Mises approximation gives
   $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\approx\mathcal J^{-1}$, equals the parameter dimension $p$ to
   leading order. The WAIC penalty satisfies the same trace formula, $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\operatorname{tr}
   (\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y))+o(1)$, so $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=p_{D}+o(1)$ and all
   three criteria agree to leading order.

3. **(Parameterization.)** WAIC and LOO depend on $\boldsymbol\xi$ only through the pointwise densities
   $p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ and are invariant under reparameterization of $\boldsymbol\xi$; DIC depends
   on the posterior mean $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}$ through $D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$ and is not.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Strategy and vocabulary.* The whole of Part 1 is one Taylor expansion of a *cumulant generating
function*: for a random quantity $Z$, this is the function $K(t)=\log\mathbb E[e^{tZ}]$ whose derivatives
at $t=0$ are the *cumulants* of $Z$ (the first cumulant is the mean, the second the variance, the third
$\kappa_3$ a measure of skewness). The one trick is that the two predictive densities we must compare
turn out to be exactly $K$ evaluated at $t=+1$ and at $t=-1$, so subtracting two Taylor series does the
work.

*Part 1.* Fix $i$ and let $K_i(t)=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[e^{t\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)}]$
be the cumulant generating function of $\ell_i$ under the posterior, with $K_i(0)=0$, $K_i'(0)=m_i$,
$K_i''(0)=v_i$, and third derivative the third cumulant $\kappa_{3,i}$. By Taylor expansion,
$$
K_i(t)=m_i t+\tfrac12 v_i t^2+\tfrac16\kappa_{3,i}t^3+\cdots .
$$
Two evaluations give the two predictive densities. First, $\mathrm{lppd}_i=\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi
\mid\mathbf y}[p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]=\log\mathbb E[e^{\ell_i}]=K_i(1)=m_i+\tfrac12 v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i})$.
Second, by the leave-one-out identity @eq-comp-loo-identity,
$$
\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=-\log\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}\big[e^{-\ell_i}\big]
=-K_i(-1)=-\big(-m_i+\tfrac12 v_i-\tfrac16\kappa_{3,i}+\cdots\big)=m_i-\tfrac12 v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i}).
$$
Subtracting, $\mathrm{lppd}_i-\log p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=v_i+O(\kappa_{3,i})=v_i+o(v_i)$ under the
hypothesis $\kappa_{3,i}=o(v_i)$, which rearranges to @eq-comp-waic-loo-pointwise. Summing over $i$ and
recognizing $\sum_i v_i=p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}$ gives $\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\mathrm{lppd}-
p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}+o(1)$; multiplying by $-2$, $\mathrm{LOO}=\mathrm{WAIC}+o(1)$.

*Part 2.* Write $\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)=\log p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ and expand to second order about
the posterior mean $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}$,
$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)=\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\nabla\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top(\boldsymbol\xi-
\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})-\tfrac12(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal J\,(\boldsymbol\xi-
\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\cdots,
$$
with $\mathcal J=-\nabla^2\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$. Taking the posterior expectation and using
$\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}]=\mathbf 0$ and $\mathbb E[(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol
\xi})(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top]=\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$,
$$
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)]=\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})-\tfrac12
\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1).
$$
Since $p_D=\mathbb E[D(\boldsymbol\xi)]-D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})=-2\big(\mathbb E[\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)]-
\ell(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})\big)$, substituting gives @eq-comp-pd. Under a flat prior the posterior is
approximately $\mathcal N(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi},\mathcal J^{-1})$ (Bernstein-von Mises), so $\mathrm{Var}
(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\approx\mathcal J^{-1}$ and $p_D\approx\operatorname{tr}(I_p)=p$. For the WAIC
penalty, linearize each $\ell_i$ about $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}$: $\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)\approx\ell_i
(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+\nabla\ell_i(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top(\boldsymbol\xi-\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$, so
$v_i=\mathrm{Var}[\ell_i]\approx\nabla\ell_i^\top\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\nabla\ell_i$ and
$$
p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\sum_i v_i\approx\operatorname{tr}\!\Big(\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)
\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\nabla\ell_i^\top\Big)=\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\mathcal J\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi
\mid\mathbf y)\big)+o(1),
$$
because, when the model is correctly specified, the outer-product information $\sum_i\nabla\ell_i
\nabla\ell_i^\top$ agrees with the observed information $\mathcal J$ to leading order (the
information-matrix equality of Chapter 5). Under misspecification the two differ, and $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}$
then estimates the robust penalty $\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J^{-1}\sum_i\nabla\ell_i\nabla\ell_i^\top)$
rather than $p_D$; the statement of part 2 is for the correctly specified case. Hence $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=p_D+o(1)$ and, combined with Part 1, $\mathrm{DIC}=\mathrm{WAIC}+o(1)=
\mathrm{LOO}+o(1)$.

*Part 3.* $\mathrm{WAIC}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}$ are built only from the numbers
$\{p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}$, which are densities of the data and are unchanged by any smooth
invertible reparameterization $\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\boldsymbol\eta(\boldsymbol\xi)$ (the likelihood value
at a parameter point does not depend on the coordinates used to name that point). DIC contains
$D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$, and the posterior mean $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}$ is *not* equivariant under
nonlinear reparameterization ($\overline{\boldsymbol\eta(\boldsymbol\xi)}\neq\boldsymbol\eta(\bar
{\boldsymbol\xi})$ in general), so $D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})$, $p_D$, and DIC change under
reparameterization. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and a scorecard.** The theorem says the three criteria estimate one thing,
out-of-sample predictive accuracy, and agree to leading order, so the choice among them is about
robustness and honesty, not about targeting different quantities. For an indirect comparison you will be
asked to justify a modeling choice, say whether to include the age effect modifier $\boldsymbol\beta_2$
or which outcome model to use, and predictive criteria are the Bayesian answer. The scorecard:

| Property | DIC | WAIC | LOO (PSIS) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Estimates out-of-sample elpd | yes | yes | yes |
| Uses the whole posterior, not just its mean | no | yes | yes |
| Pointwise (per-observation, gives a standard error) | no | yes | yes |
| Invariant to reparameterization | no | yes | yes |
| Per-observation reliability diagnostic | no | no | yes ($\widehat k$) |
| Can misbehave (negative penalty on skew posteriors) | yes | rarely | flagged by $\widehat k$ |

The ranking is LOO, then WAIC, then DIC. Report WAIC or PSIS-LOO by default; report DIC only when an
older NMA analysis you must compare against reported it, and then with these caveats stated.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Comparison is not checking.** A subtle trap for the indirect-comparison analyst: a model can have the
best WAIC or LOO in a candidate set and still answer the wrong question. Predictive criteria score *fit
to the observed evidence*; they say nothing about whether the target population is right, whether the
shared-effect-modifier assumption holds, or whether the networks overlap enough to transport an effect
(Chapters 11, 12, and 17). Model *checking*, posterior predictive checks, prior-sensitivity analysis,
and covariate-overlap diagnostics, is a separate obligation that must be met *before* model *comparison*
is meaningful. Good LOO on a model that violates transportability is a precise answer to the wrong
question.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Computation and recommendation.** Every quantity here is computed from the posterior draws
$\{\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^S$ by replacing posterior expectations with sample averages:
$\mathrm{lppd}_i\approx\log\big(\tfrac1S\sum_s p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\big)$ and $v_i\approx$ the
sample variance of $\{\log p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}_s$. WAIC and LOO are pointwise (a contribution
per observation), which yields a standard error for the criterion and for differences between models, and
flags individual influential observations; DIC offers neither. Because DIC further depends on the
non-equivariant posterior mean and can return a negative $p_D$ for skewed posteriors, current practice
prefers WAIC or, better, the LOO-CV of the next section, which estimates the same elpd while leaving each
observation genuinely out. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.5 in the proof catalogue, and to result D.14 (the DIC decomposition) of
Chapter 15.

## Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO {#sec-comp-psis}

The leave-one-out identity @eq-comp-loo-identity expresses $p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})$ as a posterior
expectation, hence as a single Monte Carlo average over the draws we already have, with no refitting. The
catch is that the importance ratios $r_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ are heavy-tailed: they
are largest exactly where the $i$-th likelihood is smallest, in regions the full posterior visits rarely,
so a few draws can dominate the sum and inflate its variance, sometimes to infinity. Pareto-smoothed
importance sampling (PSIS) repairs the tail and, as a by-product, returns a diagnostic that says when the
repair can be trusted. This is catalogue result I.6.

::: {#def-psis-loo}
## Pareto-smoothed importance sampling LOO
Given posterior draws $\{\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}\}_{s=1}^S$ from the full posterior, form for each observation
$i$ the raw importance ratios $r_i^{(s)}=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$. **PSIS** proceeds:

1. Fit a generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) to the largest ratios (the upper tail, in practice the top
   $20\%$ or the top $\min\{0.2S,\,3\sqrt S\}$ ratios), obtaining a shape estimate $\widehat k$ and scale
   estimate.
2. Replace those largest ratios by the expected GPD order statistics implied by the fit, and cap all
   ratios at the largest fitted value (smoothing and truncation), giving stabilized weights $\bar
   r_i^{(s)}$.
3. Estimate the leave-one-out predictive density by the self-normalized importance average of
   @eq-comp-is,
   $$
   \widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=\frac{\sum_{s}\bar r_i^{(s)}\,p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})}
   {\sum_{s}\bar r_i^{(s)}},
   $$ {#eq-comp-psis}
   and report $\mathrm{PSIS\text{-}LOO}=-2\sum_i\log\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})$.

The fitted shape $\widehat k_i$ is retained as a per-observation reliability diagnostic. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation: what is being smoothed, and what $\widehat k$ measures.** To reuse one posterior
fit as if we had refit it without observation $i$, we reweight the draws by $r_i=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol
\xi)$: draws where the model fit $y_i$ badly (small $p$) get large weight, because those are the draws
the without-$i$ posterior would favor. The danger is a handful of draws with tiny $p(y_i\mid\cdot)$ and
therefore enormous weights that swamp the sum, the way a single lottery winner swamps the mean income of
a room. The *generalized Pareto distribution* (GPD) is the standard model for the extreme upper tail of
such weights; its *shape* parameter $k$ measures how heavy that tail is (larger $k$ means a heavier
tail, more prone to one dominating weight). PSIS fits a GPD to the largest weights, replaces them with
the tamer values the fit predicts, and returns $\widehat k$ as a thermometer for how dangerous the tail
was. A large $\widehat k$ says the reweighting is untrustworthy *and*, substantively, that unit $i$ is
influential.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

That the raw ratios are the correct importance weights is exactly @lem-comp-loo-identity: $r_i\propto
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})/\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$, so @eq-comp-is targets the
leave-one-out posterior. The reason smoothing is needed, and the meaning of the thresholds on $\widehat
k$, both follow from a single fact about the moments of a Pareto tail.

::: {#lem-comp-gpd-moments}
## Moments of a generalized Pareto tail
Let $X$ have a generalized Pareto upper tail with shape $k>0$ and scale $\sigma>0$, that is survival
function $\bar F(x)=(1+k x/\sigma)^{-1/k}$ for $x\ge 0$. Then $\mathbb E[X^{m}]<\infty$ if and only if
$m<1/k$. In particular the mean is finite iff $k<1$ and the variance is finite iff $k<1/2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The density is $f(x)=\tfrac1\sigma(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}$, so as $x\to\infty$, $f(x)\sim C\,x^{-1/k-1}$ for
a positive constant $C$ (since $(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}\sim(kx/\sigma)^{-1/k-1}$). The $m$-th moment is
$\int_0^\infty x^m f(x)\,dx$; its convergence is determined by the integrand's decay at infinity, where
$x^m f(x)\sim C\,x^{m-1/k-1}$. The integral $\int^{\infty}x^{m-1/k-1}\,dx$ converges if and only if the
exponent is below $-1$, that is $m-1/k-1<-1$, equivalently $m<1/k$. Setting $m=1$ gives finiteness of the
mean iff $k<1$, and $m=2$ gives finiteness of the variance iff $k<1/2$. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-comp-psis-reliability}
## The shape parameter governs reliability
Let the importance ratios $r_i$ have a generalized Pareto upper tail with shape $\widehat k_i$. Then:

1. if $\widehat k_i<\tfrac12$, the ratios have finite variance, the central limit theorem applies to the
