   importance estimator, and the PSIS-LOO estimate @eq-comp-psis is reliable;
2. if $\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1$, the ratios have finite mean but infinite variance, so the raw estimator
   has no $\sqrt S$ central-limit guarantee, although PSIS smoothing keeps the bias and variance moderate
   in practice up to about $\widehat k_i\approx 0.7$;
3. if $\widehat k_i\ge 1$, even the mean is infinite and the importance estimate is unusable; that
   observation must be evaluated by actually refitting the model without it.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-comp-gpd-moments the second moment of $r_i$ is finite iff $\widehat k_i<\tfrac12$, which is the
classical condition for a $\sqrt S$ central limit theorem for the self-normalized importance estimator
@eq-comp-is; this gives (1). For $\tfrac12\le\widehat k_i<1$ the same lemma gives a finite mean but an
infinite variance, so the importance average still converges to the right value by the law of large
numbers but without a Gaussian error rate; the residual usefulness up to $\widehat k_i\approx 0.7$ is the
empirical finding that PSIS truncation and smoothing reduce the finite-sample error enough to be tolerable
in that range, which is why $0.7$ rather than $0.5$ is the operational alarm. For $\widehat k_i\ge 1$ the
mean is infinite, the importance estimator does not even converge to a finite limit, and refitting is the
only recourse; this is (3). $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters: an influential study in the running network.** Suppose the fitted model reports
$\widehat k=0.8$ for the aggregate $BC$ arm and $\widehat k<0.5$ everywhere else. Read it twice, exactly
as @thm-comp-psis-reliability licenses. As a *computational* warning, $0.8$ exceeds the $0.7$ alarm, so
the PSIS-LOO contribution of that arm is unreliable and should be recomputed by actually refitting
without it. As a *substantive* signal, it says the $d_{BC}$ contrast, and therefore the indirect $d_{AC}$
that depends on it, rests heavily on this one study. Here the flagged unit is one of the only two arms that
inform $C$, so leaving it out makes $d_{AC}$ unidentifiable: the high $\widehat k$ simply records that the
indirect comparison rests on this study, and the appropriate robustness analysis varies that study's
inputs (its reconstructed covariate distribution, its outcome model) rather than deleting it. A high $\widehat
k$ is thus not only a caution about a number; it is the diagnostic pointing at the study your conclusion
leans on.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the harmonic-mean estimator fails, and PSIS as the fix.** Setting all weights equal in
@eq-comp-loo-identity recovers the notorious harmonic-mean estimator $\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=
S/\sum_s 1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$, whose ratios $r_i$ typically have $\widehat k_i>\tfrac12$ and
sometimes $\widehat k_i\ge 1$; it is unstable precisely for the reason @thm-comp-psis-reliability isolates.
PSIS replaces the offending upper tail of the $r_i$ by the smooth GPD fit, which both stabilizes the
estimate and yields $\widehat k_i$ as a calibrated warning light. For ML-NMR and its unanchored extension,
$\widehat k_i$ flags aggregate cells or studies whose removal would most change the fit, so a large
$\widehat k_i$ is read twice: as a caution about the LOO number and as a substantive indication of an
influential or poorly-fit data point. PSIS-LOO is the default method of the standard cross-validation
software and the recommended criterion for these models. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**No machine-checked counterpart.** None of the results of this chapter has a counterpart in the
companion Coq development; the formalized tree ends with the algebraic content of population adjustment,
and the computational and diagnostic material here is established by the proofs above and validated
empirically rather than by mechanized proof. No theorem in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This development corresponds to I.6 in the proof catalogue.

## How to use this chapter in practice: a diagnostic workflow {#sec-comp-workflow}

The results above prove that each diagnostic does what it claims. This section assembles them into the
order a health researcher should actually run, and into a single table to consult when one fires. The
ordering principle is that model *comparison* is meaningless until the fit is *computationally*
trustworthy, which is meaningless until the model has passed *checking*. So the sequence runs
computation, then checking, then comparison, and never the reverse.

*The order of operations.*

1. **Divergences and tree depth first.** Before reading any estimate, check the count of divergent
   transitions after warmup and whether trajectories are hitting the maximum tree depth. A nonzero
   divergence count is a red flag that the sampler could not enter part of the posterior; treat it as a
   geometry problem (@sec-comp-param), not a "run longer" problem.
2. **$\widehat R$ next.** Require $\widehat R\le 1.01$ for every reported quantity: contrasts, $\tau$,
   baselines, effect modifiers, and the transformed marginal probabilities. A failure here means the
   chains disagree (@sec-comp-rhat); do not read the posterior.
3. **Bulk and tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.** With convergence established, check that both exceed about
   $400$ per quantity (@sec-comp-ess). Low bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ makes the posterior mean noisy; low
   tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ makes the credible-interval endpoints noisy.
4. **Inspect the culprits.** For any parameter that failed, look at its trace and at pairs plots against
   $\log\tau$; a funnel signature (divergences bunched at small $\tau$) points to the non-centered fix.
5. **QMC doubling for aggregate cells.** Confirm the integration grid is fine enough
   (@sec-comp-integration) so that the likelihood the sampler targeted is the one you meant.
6. **Posterior predictive and assumption checks.** Only a model that fits and that respects its
   transportability and effect-modification assumptions (Chapters 11, 12, 17) is worth comparing.
7. **Then, and only then, PSIS-LOO or WAIC**, reading $\widehat k$ per unit before trusting the numbers
   (@sec-comp-psis).

*The diagnostic table.* Each row is a check; consult it when the check fires.

| Diagnostic | What it detects | Threshold and action |
|---|---|---|
| Divergent transitions | posterior geometry the sampler could not follow; possible bias | any after warmup is a warning; non-center, raise `adapt_delta`, tighten the prior on $\tau$, rescale covariates |
| Max tree depth hit | trajectories truncated; inefficiency, not bias | raise the limit; usually a curvature symptom |
| $\widehat R$ | chains disagree (unconverged, multimodal, drifting) | require $\le 1.01$; if not, more warmup or reparameterize |
| Bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | noisy posterior *mean* from autocorrelation | aim $\ge 400$; run longer or improve mixing |
| Tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | noisy *credible-interval endpoints* | aim $\ge 400$; matters when you report $2.5\%$ and $97.5\%$ limits |
| QMC doubling increment | integration grid too coarse inside the likelihood | require $<\epsilon$ (say $0.005$); double $N$ |
| Pareto $\widehat k$ | unreliable LOO *and* an influential unit | $<0.7$ trust; $\ge 0.7$ refit without that unit |
| Model-comparison SE | difference in WAIC or LOO within noise | compare the difference to its standard error before ranking models |

*Divergences in depth, because they are the check most often mishandled.* A divergence is the leapfrog
integrator's report that it lost the trajectory: the simulated energy jumped by more than a threshold, so
the proposed move was discarded and, more importantly, a region of the posterior was left unexplored. Two
consequences follow. First, divergences usually signal *geometry, not too few iterations*: running four
times as long reproduces them in the same place. The remedies are the ones this chapter derived or named,
the non-centered parameterization when $\tau$ is weakly identified (@thm-comp-param), a higher
`adapt_delta` so warmup chooses a smaller step size, a tighter prior on $\tau$ to keep the chain out of
the extreme neck, and rescaling covariates so the mass matrix can round the geometry. Second, *a few
divergences are not negligible*: because they concentrate exactly where the geometry is worst, often at
small $\tau$, the parameters most affected are the heterogeneity and the study effects tied to it, which
for a sparse network are the very quantities the indirect comparison is most sensitive to. The correct
reaction to "12 divergences" is to find where they sit and remove their cause, not to report the fit with
a footnote.

*Reading a real summary table.* Software returns a table like the following, a plausible fit of the
running network with the age effect modifier included. Every column is a diagnostic from this chapter.

| Parameter | mean | sd | bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | $\widehat R$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $d_{AC}$ ($C$ vs $A$, log-odds) | $-0.42$ | $0.28$ | $2100$ | $1850$ | $1.001$ |
| $d_{AB}$ | $-0.55$ | $0.19$ | $3200$ | $2900$ | $1.000$ |
| $d_{BC}$ | $0.13$ | $0.21$ | $2600$ | $2400$ | $1.001$ |
| $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,\text{age}}$ | $-0.08$ | $0.11$ | $1900$ | $1700$ | $1.002$ |
| $\mu_{AB}$ | $-1.20$ | $0.15$ | $2800$ | $2500$ | $1.001$ |
| $\tau$ | $0.31$ | $0.24$ | $90$ | $140$ | $1.08$ |

Read it top to bottom. The contrasts and the effect modifier are healthy: $\widehat R=1.00$, several
thousand effective draws, so the reported $d_{AC}=-0.42$ (an odds ratio of about $0.66$ for $C$ versus
$A$) is stable and precise. The last row is the failure the whole chapter anticipates: $\tau$ has
$\widehat R=1.08\gg 1.01$ and only $90$ bulk effective draws, the signature of a residual funnel in a
one-study-per-contrast network. Reported alongside, say, "14 divergent transitions, all at $\tau<0.1$,"
the diagnosis is unambiguous. The fix is not to publish $d_{AC}$ with a caveat; it is to refit under the
non-centered parameterization (already the default here, so one would instead tighten the prior on $\tau$
and raise `adapt_delta`), confirm the divergences vanish and $\tau$'s $\widehat R$ falls below $1.01$, and
only then read the contrast. That is what "checking whether an indirect comparison fit can be trusted"
concretely means.

## A worked diagnostic example {#sec-comp-example}

We run the full diagnostic battery on a small, hand-checkable instance, mimicking the report one would
produce for a fitted ML-NMR model: convergence ($\widehat R$), efficiency ($N_{\mathrm{eff}}$),
integration error (the doubling rule), and model comparison (WAIC and PSIS-LOO). Every number can be
reproduced with a calculator.

::: {#exm-comp-diagnostics}
## A complete diagnostic report

The numbers here are deliberately tiny so every step is checkable by hand: read each block as the
hand-computation behind one row of the summary table of @sec-comp-workflow, applied to the running
network. Here $\theta=d_{AB}$ is the $A$-versus-$B$ log-odds contrast, and the two fitted observations
stand for one IPD patient and one aggregate arm.

**Convergence: $\widehat R$.** Two chains of length $N=4$ are run for a treatment contrast $\theta=d_{AB}$,
giving the post-warmup draws
$$
\text{chain 1: }(2,4,6,8),\qquad \text{chain 2: }(4,6,8,10).
$$
The chain means are $\bar\theta^{(1)}=5$ and $\bar\theta^{(2)}=7$, grand mean $\bar{\bar\theta}=6$. Each
chain has the same sample variance, $s_m^2=\frac{1}{3}\big[(\pm3)^2+(\pm1)^2\big]=\frac{1}{3}(9+1+1+9)=
\frac{20}{3}$, so $W=\frac{20}{3}\approx 6.667$. The between-chain variance is $B=\frac{N}{M-1}\big[(5-6)^2
+(7-6)^2\big]=\frac{4}{1}(1+1)=8$. The pooled estimator is
$$
\widehat V=\Big(1-\tfrac14\Big)\tfrac{20}{3}+\tfrac14\cdot 8=5+2=7,
\qquad
\widehat R=\sqrt{\widehat V/W}=\sqrt{\tfrac{7}{20/3}}=\sqrt{\tfrac{21}{20}}=\sqrt{1.05}\approx 1.025 .
$$
With $\widehat R\approx 1.025>1.01$ the chains have not converged: the systematic offset between the chain
means (5 versus 7) inflates $\widehat V$ above $W$, exactly the mechanism of part 3 of @thm-gelman-rubin.
The remedy is more warmup or a better parameterization (@sec-comp-param), after which $\widehat R$ should
fall below $1.01$.

**Efficiency: $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$.** Suppose the converged chains behave like an AR(1) process. With lag-1
autocorrelation $\phi=\tfrac13$, @exm-comp-ar1 gives $\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{1+1/3}{1-1/3}=2$ and
efficiency $\tfrac12$, so $4000$ total draws are worth $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2000$ independent draws; the Monte
Carlo standard error of the posterior mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{2000}$. A stickier chain with $\phi=0.9$ gives
$\tau_{\mathrm{int}}=19$ and $N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 210$, below the working threshold of $400$ and a
signal to run longer or improve mixing.

**Integration error: the doubling rule.** A logit-link aggregate cell requires
$\theta=\int_0^1\operatorname{expit}\!\big(0.4+0.8\,\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)\,du$, the marginal event
probability when the linear predictor is normal with mean $0.4$ and standard deviation $0.8$. We integrate
with the one-dimensional Sobol' sequence (the van der Corput sequence in base $2$, @def-sobol-net), whose
first points are $u_1=\tfrac12,\,u_2=\tfrac14,\,u_3=\tfrac34,\,u_4=\tfrac18,\dots$; the first eight
integrand values are
$$
0.599,\ 0.465,\ 0.719,\ 0.373,\ 0.658,\ 0.536,\ 0.789,\ 0.304,
$$
averaging to $\widehat\theta^{(8)}=0.5554$. Doubling the grid gives the sequence
$$
\widehat\theta^{(16)}=0.5683,\quad \widehat\theta^{(32)}=0.5765,\quad \widehat\theta^{(64)}=0.5812,
\quad \widehat\theta^{(128)}=0.5838,\quad \widehat\theta^{(256)}=0.5853,
$$
converging to the exact value $\theta=0.5868$ (computable independently by high-order Gauss-Hermite
quadrature). The relative doubling increments @eq-comp-doubling are
$$
\frac{|0.5812-0.5765|}{0.5812}=0.0082,\quad
\frac{|0.5838-0.5812|}{0.5838}=0.0045,\quad
\frac{|0.5853-0.5838|}{0.5853}=0.0024 .
$$
At tolerance $\epsilon=0.005$ the criterion first passes at $N=128$ (increment $0.0045<0.005$), and the
next doubling confirms it ($0.0024$). The true relative error at $N=128$ is $|0.5838-0.5868|/0.5868=
0.0051$, consistent with the bound of @prp-comp-doubling at $\rho\approx\tfrac12$, which predicts a true
relative error near the observed increment. So $N=128$ points suffice for this cell at this tolerance.

**Model comparison: WAIC and PSIS-LOO.** Two observations are fit, and the pointwise likelihoods at $S=4$
posterior draws are
$$
p(y_1\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.4,0.5,0.5,0.6\},\qquad
p(y_2\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.2,0.3,0.3,0.4\}.
$$
The pointwise predictive densities are the within-row means, $\bar p_1=0.5$ and $\bar p_2=0.3$, so
$$
\mathrm{lppd}=\log 0.5+\log 0.3=-0.6931-1.2040=-1.8971 .
$$
The WAIC penalties are the within-row sample variances of the log likelihoods. For $y_1$, the logs are
$(-0.9163,-0.6931,-0.6931,-0.5108)$ with mean $-0.7033$ and sample variance $v_1=0.02754$; for $y_2$, the
logs are $(-1.6094,-1.2040,-1.2040,-0.9163)$ with mean $-1.2334$ and sample variance $v_2=0.08123$. Hence
$p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=v_1+v_2=0.1088$ and
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=\mathrm{lppd}-p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}=-2.0059,\qquad
\mathrm{WAIC}=-2\,(-2.0059)=4.012 .
$$
For LOO, the raw importance ratios are $r_i^{(s)}=1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$, and because
$p\cdot r=1$ the self-normalized estimate @eq-comp-psis with raw weights reduces to the harmonic mean
$\widehat p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=S/\sum_s r_i^{(s)}$. For $y_1$, $\sum_s r_1^{(s)}=2.5+2+2+1.667=8.167$,
so $\widehat p_1=4/8.167=0.4898$; for $y_2$, $\sum_s r_2^{(s)}=5+3.333+3.333+2.5=14.167$, so $\widehat
p_2=4/14.167=0.2824$. Then
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{elpd}}_{\mathrm{loo}}=\log 0.4898+\log 0.2824=-0.7137-1.2645=-1.9782,\qquad
\mathrm{LOO}=3.956 .
$$
The two criteria agree to within $4.012-3.956=0.056$ on the deviance scale, illustrating the asymptotic
equivalence of part 1 of @thm-dic-waic-loo even at this tiny sample size; the small gap is the
higher-order $o(v_i)$ term. With only $S=4$ draws a generalized Pareto tail cannot be fit, so $\widehat k$
is not reported here; in a real fit with thousands of draws one would read $\widehat k_i$ for each
observation against the $0.7$ alarm of @thm-comp-psis-reliability before trusting the LOO numbers.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-comp-notes}

The chapter expands results I.1 to I.6 of the proof catalogue (`proofs/I_computation.md`) and the companion
manuscript chapter on Bayesian computation, supplying complete proofs and the worked example. The
underlying Bayesian-foundations results it draws on, Bayes' theorem, conjugacy, the posterior predictive,
and the detailed-balance correctness of HMC, are catalogue results L.1 to L.4, proved in Chapter 8
(@thm-mh-stationarity, @def-hmc, @thm-conjugate-normal); the numerical-integration machinery it monitors,
the Koksma-Hlawka inequality and the Sobol' construction, are catalogue results H.12 to H.19 of Chapter 22
(@thm-koksma-hlawka, @thm-mc-rmse, @def-sobol-net, @thm-hypercube-integration); and the aggregation
integral whose evaluation is at stake is the subject of Chapter 20 (@thm-aggregation, @thm-log-link-mgf,
@thm-logit-no-closed-form). The DIC decomposition $\mathrm{DIC}=D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})+2p_D$ is catalogue
result D.14, introduced for network meta-analysis in Chapter 15.

The centered-versus-non-centered analysis and the funnel pathology it addresses are standard in the
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo literature; the leapfrog stability threshold $\epsilon\omega<2$
(@lem-comp-leapfrog-stability) is the linear-stability analysis of the Stormer-Verlet integrator, and the
funnel as the canonical hierarchical-model trap is due to Neal. The implementation of HMC and the No-U-Turn
Sampler used by the reference ML-NMR software, including the automatic step-size and mass-matrix
adaptation, is Stan (@carpenter2017stan). The Gelman-Rubin statistic is the original convergence
diagnostic of Gelman and Rubin; the exact expectation identities $\mathbb E[\widehat V]=\sigma^2$ and
$\mathbb E[W]=\frac{N}{N-1}(\sigma^2-v_N)$ derived here (@thm-gelman-rubin) make precise the "$\widehat V$
overestimates, $W$ underestimates" intuition, and the split and rank-normalized refinements are the modern
reassessment of Vehtari and coauthors, who also introduced the bulk/tail effective sample sizes of
@sec-comp-ess. The variance-of-the-mean identity @eq-comp-var-mean and the integrated autocorrelation time
are classical time-series facts (see, for example, the MCMC standard-error literature of Geyer). The
predictive-criterion framework, elpd as the target and lppd as its optimistic in-sample estimate, is due to
Watanabe (WAIC) and to the cross-validation synthesis of Vehtari, Gelman, and Gabry; the exact
leave-one-out importance identity @eq-comp-loo-identity and the Pareto-smoothing algorithm with its
$\widehat k$ diagnostic (@def-psis-loo, @thm-comp-psis-reliability) are from the PSIS-LOO papers of that
group, and the generalized-Pareto moment characterization @lem-comp-gpd-moments is elementary extreme-value
theory.

The proofs given here are pen-and-paper throughout. As recorded in the remark closing @sec-comp-psis, none
of this material has a machine-checked counterpart in the `ITC_Coq` development, whose formalized content
ends with population-adjustment algebra; accordingly no theorem in this chapter carries a machine-checked
tag.

## Exercises {#sec-comp-exercises}

An exercise marked $\star$ has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are warm-ups: read a
diagnostic report and decide what to do, before any algebra.

::: {#exr-comp-read-table}
## Reading a Stan summary (warm-up, interpretation)
A fitted ML-NMR model reports, for the contrast $d_{AC}$: $\widehat R=1.00$, bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=2200$,
tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=1900$; and for the heterogeneity $\tau$: $\widehat R=1.06$, bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}
=110$, tail $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=160$, with $9$ divergent transitions reported, all at small $\tau$. In
words, and without any calculation: which quantity do you trust, which do you not, what single mechanism
from @sec-comp-param most likely explains the pattern, and what would you change before reporting
$d_{AC}$? Explain why "just run the chains four times longer" is the wrong first move.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-classify}
## Classify the diagnostics (warm-up, interpretation)
For each finding, state whether it is a hard failure that blocks reporting, a warning that needs
investigation, or acceptable, and name the action, using the table of @sec-comp-workflow: (a) $\widehat
R=1.004$ on every parameter; (b) bulk $N_{\mathrm{eff}}=95$ on a treatment contrast; (c) Pareto
$\widehat k=0.9$ on one aggregate arm; (d) a QMC doubling increment of $0.012$ at tolerance
$\epsilon=0.005$; (e) a WAIC difference between two models that is half the size of its standard error.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-rhat}
## Computing $\widehat R$
Three chains of length $N=5$ give the draws $(1,2,3,4,5)$, $(2,3,4,5,6)$, and $(3,4,5,6,7)$. Compute $W$,
$B$, $\widehat V$, and $\widehat R$. Does the run pass the $\widehat R\le 1.01$ threshold? Explain, using
@thm-gelman-rubin, why the answer is driven entirely by the spacing of the chain means.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-rhat-floor}
## A deterministic lower bound for $\widehat R$ $(\star)$
Show from the definitions @eq-comp-wb and @eq-comp-vhat that $\widehat V/W=\frac{N-1}{N}+\frac{B}{NW}$, and
deduce that $\widehat R\ge\sqrt{(N-1)/N}$ always, with $\widehat R\ge 1$ if and only if $B\ge W$. Using the
stationarity expectations of @lem-comp-within and @lem-comp-between, show that at convergence
$\mathbb E[B]=\mathbb E[W]$ in the iid-within-chain idealization, so that $\widehat R$ is centered at $1$,
and identify the term that pushes it above $1$ when the chains are positively autocorrelated but share a
common stationary law. (Solution in Appendix F.)
:::

::: {#exr-comp-ess-acf}
## Effective sample size from an autocorrelation sequence
A chain has estimated autocorrelations $\rho_1=0.6$, $\rho_2=0.36$, $\rho_3=0.216$, and $\rho_k=0.6^k$
thereafter. Using @def-mcmc-ess, compute the integrated autocorrelation time and the efficiency
$N_{\mathrm{eff}}/N$. Compare with the AR(1) formula of @exm-comp-ar1 and explain why they coincide.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-leapfrog}
## Leapfrog stability and the funnel
A centered hierarchical effect has prior-dominated curvature $1/\tau^2$ (@lem-comp-funnel). Using
@lem-comp-leapfrog-stability, find the largest stable leapfrog step $\epsilon_{\max}(\tau)$. If the
posterior of $\tau$ ranges over $[0.05,2]$ and a single global $\epsilon$ must be stable everywhere, what
is the largest admissible $\epsilon$, and by what factor is it smaller than the step that would be
efficient at the typical value $\tau=1$? Repeat for the non-centered parameterization and comment.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-doubling}
## The doubling rule on a known integral
For $\theta=\int_0^1 u^2\,du=\tfrac13$, compute the one-dimensional Sobol' (van der Corput) estimates
$\widehat\theta^{(N)}$ for $N\in\{2,4,8,16\}$, evaluate the relative doubling increments
@eq-comp-doubling, and report the smallest $N$ at which the criterion passes at $\epsilon=0.01$. Compare the
observed errors $|\widehat\theta^{(N)}-\tfrac13|$ with the increments and comment in the light of
@prp-comp-doubling.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-loo-identity}
## The leave-one-out identity
Prove the special case $\psi=p(y_i\mid\cdot)$ of @eq-comp-is directly: starting from
$\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y_{-i})\propto\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$,
show that $p(y_i\mid\mathbf y_{-i})=1/\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[1/p(y_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi)]$.
Then explain in one sentence why estimating this by the sample harmonic mean of the draw-wise likelihoods
can have infinite variance.
:::

::: {#exr-comp-waic-loo}
## WAIC and LOO on a small posterior
Three posterior draws give pointwise likelihoods $p(y_1\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}$ and
$p(y_2\mid\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\in\{0.4,0.4,0.4\}$. Compute $\mathrm{lppd}$, $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}$, and
$\mathrm{WAIC}$, and the raw-importance-sampling $\mathrm{LOO}$. Why is the second observation's
contribution to $p_{\mathrm{WAIC}}$ exactly zero, and what does that say about its influence?
:::

::: {#exr-comp-gpd}
## Pareto tails and importance-sampling reliability $(\star)$
Let $X$ have the generalized Pareto upper tail $\bar F(x)=(1+kx/\sigma)^{-1/k}$ with $k>0$. Prove that
$\mathbb E[X^m]<\infty$ if and only if $m<1/k$ (@lem-comp-gpd-moments). Deduce the variance-finiteness
threshold $k<\tfrac12$ and the mean-finiteness threshold $k<1$, and relate them to the PSIS-LOO diagnostic
thresholds of @thm-comp-psis-reliability. Explain why the operational alarm is set at $\widehat k=0.7$
rather than at the theoretical variance threshold $0.5$. (Solution in Appendix F.)
:::
